standard.title: Cells, Tissues, Organs and Systems
standard.description: analyse the relationship between structure and function of cells, tissues and organs in a plant and an animal organ system and explain how these systems enable survival of the individual
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify and describe the function of organelles in plant and animal cells (AC9S8U01). They have not yet connected cell-level structure to tissue and organ-level function, or examined how organ systems operate as integrated units to support survival.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students analyse the structure-function relationship across the hierarchy from cell to tissue to organ to system in both a plant and an animal organ system, and explain how each level of organisation contributes to the system's role in supporting the organism's survival.

nodes.label: Cells, tissues and organs form a structural hierarchy
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the organisational hierarchy from cell → tissue → organ → organ system and explain how each level is made up of the level below, with the structural properties of each level arising from its component units.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe the four levels of biological organisation (cell, tissue, organ, organ system) and give one example of each from a named organ system.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain how specialised cells form tissues, how tissues with complementary functions combine to form organs, and how organs work together in a system — tracing this hierarchy through at least one complete plant and one complete animal organ system.
wider: Compare the structural hierarchy in a plant system (e.g. vascular system: xylem cells → vascular tissue → stem/root/leaf → transport system) with an animal system (e.g. circulatory: cardiac muscle cells → heart muscle tissue → heart → circulatory system)
Examine single-celled organisms and explain why they do not have tissues or organs — using this contrast to clarify why multicellular hierarchy is necessary at scale
Research how a disorder at the cell or tissue level propagates to organ dysfunction — e.g. how hardening of arterial tissue affects the cardiovascular system's ability to maintain circulation
nodes.hinge_reason: Without the hierarchy logic — that each level's properties emerge from the level below — students cannot analyse structure-function relationships at specific levels in Node 2. Students who treat cell, tissue, organ and system as a vocabulary list cannot explain why a tissue's function depends on its constituent cells, which is the analytical move required at Node 2.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly treat cell, tissue, organ and system as a vocabulary list rather than as a nested structural hierarchy where each level's properties emerge from the level below. Making the emergence logic explicit — specialised cells → tissue with a collective function → organ integrating tissue functions → system coordinating organ functions — is necessary before students can analyse structure-function relationships at each level.

success_criteria: Describes the four levels of biological organisation in sequence with an example from a named organ system
Explains how the function of a tissue depends on the specialised cells it contains

nodes.label: Structure determines function at each level
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can analyse the relationship between the physical structure of cells, tissues and organs and the function they perform — explaining how structural features enable function in at least one plant and one animal organ system.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two structure-function relationships in a named organ system — explaining how a specific structural feature enables a specific function.
nodes.typical_width: Students analyse structure-function relationships across multiple levels (cell, tissue, organ) in both a plant and an animal organ system, explaining how structural features at each level contribute to the overall function of the system.
wider: Compare analogous systems in a plant and an animal (e.g. plant vascular system and animal circulatory system) — examining how different structural solutions achieve the same functional goal of transporting materials
Investigate how an artificial organ mimics or augments the function of a real organ, identifying which structural features are replicated and which are not

Examine how disorders at the structural level (e.g. hardening of arteries, damage to photosynthetic cells) cascade to affect system function — applying structure-function reasoning in a pathology context

response_modes.reason: Students tend to describe structure and function as separate features rather than as a relationship — they list structural features and then separately list functions without connecting them. Analysing structure-function relationships across both plant and animal systems, and at multiple organisational levels, helps students build a more generalisable analytical approach rather than a collection of isolated examples.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Comparing plant and animal systems that achieve the same functional goal through different structural solutions is a genuinely rich analytical direction. The artificial organ direction connects structure-function reasoning to real biomedical engineering applications and links to AC9S8H01/H03.
success_criteria: Explains at least two structure-function relationships in a named organ system — connecting a specific structural feature to the function it enables
Analyses structure-function relationships in both a plant organ system and an animal organ system

nodes.label: Organ systems enable survival of the individual
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain how the functions of an organ system contribute to the survival of the individual organism — connecting system-level function to the basic survival needs of the organism (obtaining energy, removing waste, responding to the environment, reproducing).
nodes.minimum_width: Students explain how one named organ system contributes to the survival of the organism, naming at least two survival needs the system meets.
nodes.typical_width: Students explain how both a plant and an animal organ system contribute to survival, describing how each system's function addresses specific survival requirements and how a failure in the system would threaten survival.
wider: Research how a disorder in cells or tissues leads to organ dysfunction and ultimately threatens individual survival — tracing the cell-to-survival chain in reverse through a case study (e.g. heart disease, plant nutrient deficiency)

Investigate how the repair and replacement of organs using synthetic materials or transplantation maintains survival — examining what functional properties the replacement must replicate (connects to AC9S8H01 and H03)
Examine how 2D and 3D representations of organ systems are used to understand spatial relationships between organs — and why position within the body matters for function

response_modes.reason: Connecting organ system function to survival requires students to integrate the structure-function hierarchy with a functional purpose — what does all of this complexity ultimately achieve for the organism? Students who understand structure-function relationships at each level must now see those relationships as coordinated toward a larger goal. This is the synthesis move of the descriptor.

success_criteria: Explains how a named organ system's function contributes to at least two survival needs of the organism
Describes what would happen to survival if the organ system failed to function correctly
